hub.description: Free personality and psychology tests: 16 types (MBTI-style), Big Five, introvert or extrovert, Enneagram, love language, attachment, conflict style, career, work style, money, chronotype, pet match, anime, face shape, self-esteem, anxiety and depression. No sign-up; answers stay in your browser.
hub.lede: Eighteen free tests, from 16 personality types and the Big Five to love languages, career interests, your work style and quick mental health self-checks. No sign-up, no email. Your answers are scored in your browser and never uploaded.
about: Each test lists all of its questions on one page. Answer them, press the button, and the result appears under the questions with a short explanation and a chart of your scores.

The wellbeing checks use published screening questionnaires (Rosenberg, GAD-7, PHQ-9). The Big Five and the introvert–extrovert test use the public-domain IPIP item pool. The other tests are written for cv.cm from well-known models, and their results are a starting point for reflection, not a verdict.

faq.q: Are these tests free?
faq.a: Yes. Every test is free, with no sign-up, no email, and no paywall in front of the result.

faq.q: Are my answers saved?
faq.a: No. Scoring runs in your browser tab. The answers are not uploaded or stored, and closing the tab clears them.

faq.q: How accurate are online personality tests?
faq.a: A short self-report test describes how you see yourself today. Treat the result as a mirror for reflection, and retake it after a while: results that stay the same are the ones to trust.

faq.q: Which test should I start with?
faq.a: For a quick type, take the 16 personalities test. For the model psychologists use most, take the Big Five. For relationships, try the love language or attachment style test.

mbti.title: Free MBTI test: 16 personality types in 32 questions — cv.cm
mbti.description: Take a free MBTI-style personality test. Answer 32 statements and get your four-letter type (like INFJ or ESTP) with the strength of each preference. No sign-up.
mbti.lede: Find your four-letter type: where you get energy (E/I), how you take in information (S/N), how you decide (T/F), and how you organize your life (J/P).
about: The 16 types come from Carl Jung's theory of psychological types, later developed by Katharine Briggs and Isabel Myers. Each letter is one side of a pair, and the percentages show how strongly you lean that way. A result near 50% means you use both sides.
This is an independent, MBTI-style test written for cv.cm. It is not the official Myers-Briggs Type Indicator® assessment and is not affiliated with The Myers-Briggs Company.

faq.q: Is this the official MBTI test?
faq.a: No. The official MBTI® assessment is sold through certified practitioners. This free test uses the same four preference pairs with its own questions.

faq.q: What do the four letters mean?
faq.a: E or I: Extraversion or Introversion. S or N: Sensing or Intuition. T or F: Thinking or Feeling. J or P: Judging or Perceiving.

faq.q: Why did I get a different type last time?
faq.a: If one pair is close to 50%, a small change in your answers flips the letter. Look at the percentages: the strong preferences are the stable part of your type.

faq.q: Can my type change?
faq.a: Your core preferences tend to stay fairly stable in adulthood, but stress, a new job, or a new stage of life can shift how you answer.

ESTJ.name: ESTJ · The Supervisor
ESTJ.body: Practical, organized and direct. You like clear rules, get things done on time, and naturally take charge of people and projects. Watch out for steamrolling quieter voices; asking how people feel makes your plans land better.

ESTP.name: ESTP · The Doer

ESFJ.name: ESFJ · The Caregiver
ESFJ.body: Warm, loyal and sociable. You notice what people need, keep traditions alive, and hold groups together. You may take criticism to heart; remember that saying no sometimes is also a way of caring.

ESFP.name: ESFP · The Performer
ESFP.body: Fun-loving, spontaneous and generous. You bring energy into any room and enjoy the present moment with others. Planning ahead feels dull, but a little structure gives you more freedom later.

ENTJ.name: ENTJ · The Commander
ENTJ.body: Strategic, decisive and ambitious. You see how things should work, set big goals, and organize people to reach them. Patience with slower processes and with feelings will make you an even stronger leader.

ENTP.name: ENTP · The Debater
ENTP.body: Quick-witted, curious and inventive. You love ideas, arguments and new possibilities, and you challenge assumptions for fun. Finishing projects is the hard part; pair up with someone who loves the details.

ENFJ.name: ENFJ · The Mentor
ENFJ.body: Charismatic, empathetic and inspiring. You bring out the best in people and rally them around shared values. You can overcommit to others' needs; set aside time for your own.

ENFP.name: ENFP · The Champion
ENFP.body: Enthusiastic, imaginative and warm. You see potential everywhere, connect easily with people, and chase what feels meaningful. Too many open projects can scatter your energy; pick a few and see them through.

ISTJ.name: ISTJ · The Inspector
ISTJ.body: Responsible, thorough and reliable. You keep your word, value facts and proven methods, and finish what you start. Change can feel unsettling; trying small experiments helps you adapt on your own terms.

ISTP.name: ISTP · The Craftsperson
ISTP.body: Calm, logical and practical. You like to understand how things work and fix problems with your hands or with clear analysis. You value your independence; letting people know what you think helps them trust you.

ISFJ.name: ISFJ · The Protector
ISFJ.body: Kind, dependable and observant. You remember details about people and quietly take care of them. You often put others first; your own needs deserve the same attention.

ISFP.name: ISFP · The Artist
ISFP.body: Gentle, sensitive and creative. You live by your values, enjoy beauty in the moment, and express yourself through what you make or do. Conflict drains you; speaking up early keeps small issues small.

INTJ.name: INTJ · The Architect
INTJ.body: Independent, analytical and visionary. You build long-range plans, question everything, and hold yourself to high standards. Others may find you hard to read; explaining your reasoning brings people along.

INTP.name: INTP · The Thinker
INTP.body: Curious, precise and inventive. You love theories, systems and puzzles, and you need time alone to think them through. Ideas can stay in your head; sharing a rough version early turns them into something real.

INFJ.name: INFJ · The Counselor
INFJ.body: Insightful, principled and compassionate. You sense what others feel, look for deeper meaning, and work quietly toward a better world. You may burn out from caring too much; protect your rest.

INFP.name: INFP · The Idealist
INFP.body: Thoughtful, idealistic and loyal to your values. You have a rich inner world and want your life and work to mean something. Self-criticism can hold you back; progress beats perfection.

big-five.title: Free Big Five personality test (IPIP 50 questions) — cv.cm
big-five.description: Take the free Big Five (OCEAN) personality test with the public-domain IPIP 50-item questionnaire. See your openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness and neuroticism scores. No sign-up.
big-five.lede: Measure the five traits psychologists use most: Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness and Neuroticism. 50 short statements, results as five scores out of 100.
about: The Big Five (also called the Five-Factor Model or OCEAN) is the best-researched model of personality. Instead of putting you in a box, it places you on five independent scales, so everyone gets a unique profile.

This test uses the 50-item Big-Five Factor Markers from the International Personality Item Pool (IPIP), developed by Lewis Goldberg and placed in the public domain. Scores here are compared to the scale range, not to a population sample, so 50 means the middle of the scale.

faq.q: What does OCEAN stand for?
faq.a: Openness to experience, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness and Neuroticism, the five broad traits in the model.

faq.q: Is a high score better?
faq.a: No. Each end of a trait has strengths. Low extraversion goes with focus and calm; low agreeableness with candor and independence.

faq.q: Is the Big Five more scientific than MBTI?
faq.a: Most personality researchers prefer the Big Five: its traits are measured as continuous scores and predict outcomes like job performance and wellbeing in many studies.

faq.q: Where do the questions come from?
faq.a: From the IPIP 50-item Big-Five Factor Markers by Lewis Goldberg, a public-domain questionnaire used widely in research.

introvert.title: Free introvert or extrovert test (IPIP, 20 questions) — cv.cm
introvert.description: Are you an introvert, an ambivert or an extrovert? Rate 20 public-domain IPIP statements and get a score out of 80 with practical tips. Free, no sign-up.
introvert.lede: Find out where you sit between introversion and extroversion. 20 short statements from a research questionnaire, a score out of 80, and what it means for your energy, work and friendships.
about: Extraversion is one of the Big Five traits. People high in it gain energy from company, talk easily and enjoy being seen. People low in it, introverts, prefer smaller groups and quiet time, and think before they speak. Most people land somewhere in the middle: ambiverts.

The 20 statements are the extraversion scale of the 100-item Big-Five Factor Markers from the International Personality Item Pool (IPIP), developed by Lewis Goldberg and placed in the public domain. Half are reverse-scored. The cut-offs sit at 40% and 60% of the scale range (below 40% introvert, 40–60% ambivert, above 60% extrovert); they are not population norms.
Introversion is not shyness. Shyness is worry about being judged; introversion is about where your energy comes from. An introvert can be confident and socially skilled, and an extrovert can be shy.

faq.q: What is an ambivert?
faq.a: Someone in the middle of the scale: outgoing in some settings, happy alone in others. Most people are ambiverts.

faq.q: Is it better to be an extrovert?
faq.a: No. Extroverts often find networking and group work easier; introverts often do well at deep, focused work and one-to-one listening. Both can learn the skills of the other.

faq.q: Where do the questions come from?
faq.a: From the IPIP 100-item Big-Five Factor Markers by Lewis Goldberg, a public-domain item pool used widely in research. This test uses its 20 extraversion items.

faq.q: Can my result change?
faq.a: Your basic level of extraversion is fairly stable in adulthood, but it shifts a little with age, role and mood. Retake the test in a few months and compare.

Tips: plan quiet time after busy days instead of feeling guilty about it; at events, set a goal (two real conversations) and leave when it's done; offer to share ideas in writing or one-to-one, where you shine.

ambivert.name: Ambivert
ambivert.body: You sit in the middle: sociable when the setting is right, happy alone when it isn't. That flexibility is a strength: you can read a room and switch modes. Tip: notice which situations energize you and which drain you, and plan your week so neither kind piles up for too long.

extrovert.name: Extrovert
extrovert.body: You gain energy from people, talk ideas through out loud and enjoy a lively pace. Strengths: building networks, starting conversations and lifting a group. Tips: in meetings, leave room for quieter people to speak; when you need deep focus, book short sessions with a friend or coworker nearby; check in with yourself before saying yes to every invitation.

enneagram.title: Free Enneagram test: find your type in 36 questions — cv.cm
enneagram.description: Free Enneagram personality test. Rate 36 statements to see which of the nine Enneagram types fits you best, with scores for all nine. No sign-up.
enneagram.lede: Discover which of the nine Enneagram types drives you: what you want most, what you fear, and how you act under stress.
about: The Enneagram describes nine personality types, each organized around a core motivation. Most people see a little of themselves in several types; your main type is the one whose motivation feels most like home.
This short test was written for cv.cm. Read the descriptions of your top two or three types and decide which fits best: self-recognition is how the Enneagram is meant to be used.

faq.q: What are the nine Enneagram types?
faq.a: 1 Reformer, 2 Helper, 3 Achiever, 4 Individualist, 5 Investigator, 6 Loyalist, 7 Enthusiast, 8 Challenger, 9 Peacemaker.

faq.q: What is a wing?
faq.a: Your wing is one of the two types next to your main type on the Enneagram circle (a 4 can have a 3 or 5 wing). Your second-highest score is a hint if it sits next to your main type.

faq.q: My top scores are close. Which is my type?
faq.a: Read each description and ask which core fear and desire feels most true over your whole life, not just lately.

faq.q: Is the Enneagram scientific?
faq.a: Research support is limited compared with the Big Five. Many people still find it a useful language for motivation and growth.

1.name: Type 1 · The Reformer
1.body: Principled, purposeful and self-controlled. You want to be good and do things right, and you fear being corrupt or wrong. Growth comes from accepting that imperfect is often good enough, for yourself and for others.

2.name: Type 2 · The Helper
2.body: Caring, generous and people-pleasing. You want to be loved and needed, and you fear being unwanted. Growth comes from noticing your own needs and asking for help directly.

3.name: Type 3 · The Achiever
3.body: Driven, adaptable and image-conscious. You want to feel valuable and successful, and you fear being worthless. Growth comes from valuing who you are, not only what you achieve.

4.name: Type 4 · The Individualist
4.body: Expressive, sensitive and introspective. You want to find your true identity and significance, and you fear having none. Growth comes from appreciating ordinary life and what you already have.

5.name: Type 5 · The Investigator

6.name: Type 6 · The Loyalist
6.body: Committed, responsible and security-minded. You want support and guidance, and you fear being without them. Growth comes from trusting your own judgment.

7.name: Type 7 · The Enthusiast
7.body: Spontaneous, versatile and optimistic. You want to be satisfied and free, and you fear pain and missing out. Growth comes from staying with one thing, including difficult feelings.

8.name: Type 8 · The Challenger
8.body: Self-confident, decisive and protective. You want to control your own life, and you fear being harmed or controlled. Growth comes from letting trusted people see your softer side.

9.name: Type 9 · The Peacemaker
9.body: Easygoing, receptive and reassuring. You want inner and outer peace, and you fear conflict and separation. Growth comes from voicing your own priorities and acting on them.

love-language.title: Free love language test: find your love language — cv.cm
love-language.description: Free love language quiz. Rate 25 statements to see how you most like to receive love: words of affirmation, quality time, gifts, acts of service or physical touch. No sign-up.
love-language.lede: Which of the five love languages speaks to you most? Rate 25 statements and see all five ranked.
about: The idea of five love languages was popularized by counselor Gary Chapman in 1992: people tend to feel loved through words of affirmation, quality time, receiving gifts, acts of service or physical touch, and partners often speak different ones.
This independent quiz was written for cv.cm. Share your ranking with a partner or friend and ask them to take it too: knowing each other's top language is the useful part.

faq.q: What are the five love languages?
faq.a: Words of affirmation, quality time, receiving gifts, acts of service, and physical touch.

faq.q: Can I have more than one love language?
faq.a: Yes. Most people have one or two that matter most and others that matter a little. The chart shows all five.

faq.q: Is the love language idea backed by research?
faq.a: Studies give it mixed support: partners who show love in many ways tend to be happier overall. It works best as a conversation starter, not a rule.

faq.q: Is this the official quiz?
faq.a: No. It is an independent quiz built on the same five categories, not affiliated with Gary Chapman or his publisher.

attachment.title: Free attachment style test: secure, anxious or avoidant? — cv.cm
attachment.description: Free attachment style quiz for adults. Answer 16 statements about close relationships to see whether your style is secure, anxious, avoidant or fearful-avoidant. No sign-up.
attachment.lede: How do you act in close relationships? This quiz measures attachment anxiety and avoidance and places you in one of four styles.
about: Attachment theory began with John Bowlby and Mary Ainsworth's studies of children and was extended to adult romantic relationships by Hazan and Shaver. Modern research measures two dimensions: anxiety (fear of rejection) and avoidance (discomfort with closeness).

Your style comes from where you fall on both: low on both is secure. This short quiz was written for cv.cm and is based on that two-dimension model. Styles can change with time and with supportive relationships.

faq.q: What are the four attachment styles?
faq.a: Secure (low anxiety, low avoidance), anxious (high anxiety), avoidant (high avoidance), and fearful-avoidant (high on both).

faq.q: Can my attachment style change?
faq.a: Yes. A long, stable relationship, therapy, and conscious practice can move people toward security, which researchers call earned security.

faq.q: Should I answer about my current partner?
faq.a: Answer about how you generally feel in close relationships, not only about one person.

faq.q: Which style is best?
faq.a: Secure attachment is linked with the most relationship satisfaction, but every style makes sense as a response to past experience, and each can grow.

marriage.title: Free marriage readiness test for couples — cv.cm
marriage.description: Are you ready for marriage? Free 20-question quiz on communication, conflict, money, family and shared goals, with a score for each area and a tip for the weakest. No sign-up.
marriage.lede: Check how ready your relationship is for marriage across five areas counselors focus on: communication, conflict, money, family, and the future you want.
about: Premarital programs like PREPARE/ENRICH and the research of John Gottman point to the same areas: how couples talk, fight, handle money, deal with families, and agree on the future. This quiz was written for cv.cm around those five areas.
Take it separately with your partner and compare. The area where your scores differ most is the best topic for your next long conversation.

faq.q: Can a quiz tell me if I should get married?
faq.a: No. It highlights areas worth talking about. The decision depends on many things a quiz cannot see.

faq.q: Should my partner take it too?
faq.a: Yes. Answer separately, then compare your area scores. Differences are more useful than the total.

faq.q: What if we score low?
faq.a: A low score is a list of topics, not a verdict. Many couples work through them with honest talks or premarital counseling.

faq.q: Can married couples use it?
faq.a: Yes. The same five areas matter at every stage of a relationship.

ready.name: Strong foundation
ready.body: You communicate well, handle conflict and money as a team, and want a similar future. Keep investing in the habits that got you here, like regular check-ins.

close.name: Nearly there
close.body: Your relationship has a solid base with one or two areas to strengthen. Talk through the lowest area below before you take the next big step.

work.name: Some work to do
work.body: Several important topics are still unresolved. That is common. Set aside time to discuss each area, and consider a premarital course or counselor.

early.name: Early days
early.body: Many key areas haven't been worked through yet. Take time to understand each other's views on the basics before planning a wedding.

tips.talk: Try a weekly 20-minute check-in: each of you shares one high, one low and one wish, while the other only listens.
tips.conflict: Agree on a pause rule: either of you can call a 20-minute break in a heated argument, and you come back to finish it.
tips.money: Sit down with your real numbers: income, debts and savings. Then agree on one shared goal and how you will split costs.
tips.family: Discuss which family traditions and visits matter most to each of you, and present a united front to relatives.
tips.future: Each write down where you want to be in five years (home, children, careers), then compare and find the overlap.

conflict-style.title: Free conflict style test: how do you handle disagreements? — cv.cm
conflict-style.description: Free conflict style quiz. Rate 20 statements to see whether you lean toward competing, collaborating, compromising, avoiding or accommodating, and when each style helps or hurts.
conflict-style.lede: Everyone has a default move when a disagreement starts. Find yours among the five classic conflict styles, see how strongly you use the others, and learn when to switch.
about: Researchers describe five ways of handling conflict along two questions: how hard you push for your own needs (assertiveness) and how much you care about the other person's (cooperativeness). Competing is high on the first, accommodating high on the second, collaborating high on both, avoiding low on both, and compromising sits in the middle.

The statements on this page were written for cv.cm; they are not taken from any commercial instrument. Every style is useful in the right moment. The aim is not to find the "right" style but to notice your habit and choose on purpose.

faq.q: What are the five conflict styles?
faq.a: Competing (stand your ground), collaborating (solve it together so both win), compromising (meet in the middle), avoiding (step away) and accommodating (give the other person what they want).

faq.q: Which conflict style is best?
faq.a: None in every case. Collaborating suits important issues with time to talk; competing suits emergencies; compromising suits deadlocks; avoiding suits trivial or heated moments; accommodating suits issues that matter more to the other side.

faq.q: Is this the Thomas-Kilmann instrument?
faq.a: No. It uses the same widely taught five-style model, but the questions and results are original to cv.cm, and the scores are not comparable to any commercial test.

faq.q: Can I use it with my partner or team?
faq.a: Yes. Take it separately, compare charts, and talk about which styles you each fall back on under stress. Knowing the other person's default makes it easier not to take it personally.

I look for a solution that fully works for both of us, even if it takes longer.
A fair trade, where each side gives something up, feels like a good outcome to me.

Keeping the relationship smooth matters more to me than winning the point.
I treat a debate as something to win.
I ask a lot of questions to understand what the other person really needs.
When we're stuck, I suggest splitting the difference.

I often put other people's wishes ahead of my own so I don't upset them.
If a decision matters to me, I push hard for it, even if it causes some tension.

compete.name: Competing
compete.body: You stand up for your position and don't fold under pressure. Helps: emergencies, unpopular but necessary calls, protecting yourself from being taken advantage of. Hurts: when it becomes your only move, people stop telling you things and quietly resent decisions. Try: before arguing, ask one genuine question about what the other person needs, and save full force for issues that truly matter.

collab.name: Collaborating
collab.body: You want a solution that fully works for both sides, and you dig into the real interests behind each position. Helps: important decisions, long-term relationships, problems with room for creative answers. Hurts: it takes time and energy, and not every small issue deserves a workshop. Try: decide up front whether a topic is worth the full process; for minor ones, a quick compromise is fine.

compromise.name: Compromising
compromise.body: You look for a fair middle so everyone can move on. Helps: deadlocks, equal power on both sides, time pressure. Hurts: splitting the difference too fast can leave both people half-satisfied and miss a better answer. Try: before offering the middle, ask "What matters most to you here?"; you may find a trade where each side gets what it cares about most.

avoid.name: Avoiding
avoid.body: You step back from conflict, and you're good at not escalating small things. Helps: trivial issues, heated moments that need a cool-down, fights you can't win or don't need to. Hurts: important problems grow while they wait, and others may read silence as agreement. Try: when you avoid, set a time to return ("Can we talk tomorrow evening?"), and write down the one point you need to make.

accommodate.name: Accommodating
accommodate.body: You protect the relationship and let others have their way. Helps: issues that matter more to them, when you realize you're wrong, building goodwill. Hurts: if it's your default, your own needs disappear and frustration builds up. Try: before saying yes, rate how much the issue matters to you from 1 to 10; above 6, say what you want, kindly and clearly.

career.title: Free career test: Holland code (RIASEC) interest test — cv.cm
career.description: Free career aptitude test based on Holland's RIASEC model. Rate 36 activities to get your three-letter Holland code and careers that fit your interests. No sign-up.
career.lede: Find careers that fit your interests. Rate 36 activities and get your three-letter Holland code, from Realistic, Investigative, Artistic, Social, Enterprising and Conventional.
about: Psychologist John Holland found that people and work environments can be described by six interest types, known as RIASEC. People tend to be more satisfied in jobs that match their top types.

Your Holland code is your top three letters in order. Use it to explore careers: the U.S. O*NET database, for example, lists occupations by Holland code. This test was written for cv.cm and measures interests, not ability.

faq.q: What is a Holland code?
faq.a: Your three strongest interest types, in order, such as SAE or RIC. It is used by career counselors to suggest fitting jobs and fields of study.

faq.q: Should I rate activities I have never tried?
faq.a: Yes. Imagine doing the activity and rate how much you would enjoy it, not how good you would be at it.

faq.q: Does this test measure talent?
faq.a: No. It measures interest. Skills can be learned; interest predicts which work you will enjoy long enough to get good at.

faq.q: My scores are almost equal. What now?
faq.a: A flat profile means broad interests. Look at careers that combine your top types, and try short projects to see what you enjoy.

work-style.title: Free work style test: remote, hybrid or office? Solo or team? — cv.cm
work-style.description: Free work style quiz. Rate 20 statements to see whether remote, hybrid or office work suits you, how much teamwork, structure and variety you need, with practical tips.
work-style.lede: Where and how do you do your best work? Score four preferences, home or office, solo or team, structure or freedom, focus or variety, and get a tip for each.
about: Job satisfaction depends not only on what you do but on how the work is set up. This test, written for cv.cm, measures four everyday preferences: where you like to work, how much you like to work with others, how much structure you want, and whether you prefer variety or long stretches of focus.

Each score runs from 0 to 100. Below 40 leans one way, above 60 the other, and the middle is a mix. Use the result to ask better questions in job interviews ("How many days are in the office?", "How are priorities set?") and to shape the job you have.

faq.q: Does this tell me which career to choose?
faq.a: No. It describes working conditions, not fields. For career fields, take the Holland code career test, then use this one to choose between similar jobs.

faq.q: My remote score is in the middle. What does that mean?
faq.a: You'll probably be happiest in a hybrid setup: office days for meetings and people, home days for focused work.

faq.q: What if my job doesn't match my result?
faq.a: Small changes help: block focus time on your calendar, ask for one remote day, agree on clearer priorities with your manager, or swap tasks with a teammate who likes the work you don't.

faq.q: Is one work style better than another?
faq.a: No. Teams need both people who like structure and people who like freedom, both soloists and connectors. What matters is fit.

remote.low: Office: you get energy, focus and learning from being around colleagues. Look for roles with a real office culture, and if you work remotely, use a coworking space or a regular office day so you don't become isolated.
remote.mid: Hybrid: office days for meetings and people, home days for focused work. Ask employers how hybrid works in practice, and plan which tasks go on which days.
remote.high: Remote: you work well on your own schedule and don't miss the commute. Look for remote-first teams with good written communication, and protect a start and end time so work doesn't fill the whole day.

team.low: Solo: you prefer owning work end to end. Roles like specialist, analyst, writer or developer with clear ownership suit you. Agree on a few fixed check-ins so you stay in the loop without constant meetings.
team.mid: Mixed: you like time alone to do the work and time together to plan and review it. Batch meetings into one part of the day and keep the rest for focus.
team.high: Team: you think best out loud and enjoy shared goals. Look for collaborative roles such as project work, sales, teaching or product teams, and on solo tasks, pair up or hold short check-ins to stay motivated.

structure.low: Freedom: you want to decide how and when to work. Startups, freelancing and roles judged on results suit you. Set your own deadlines and share them, so freedom doesn't turn into last-minute stress.
structure.mid: Balanced: you like clear goals but some say in how to reach them. Ask managers for the "what" and "by when", and propose the "how" yourself.
structure.high: Structure: clear expectations, processes and priorities calm you and help you do excellent work. Larger organizations and process-driven roles suit you; when things are vague, ask early for a checklist or definition of done.

variety.low: Deep focus: you do your best work in long, uninterrupted blocks. Book two- or three-hour focus blocks, turn off notifications, and look for roles that value depth such as research, engineering or editing.
variety.mid: Balanced: some variety keeps you fresh, but too much switching wears you down. Group similar tasks together and give each day one main focus.
variety.high: Variety: new problems and a fast pace energize you, and routine bores you. Roles in operations, client work, events or startups fit; keep a simple list so many threads don't slip.

money.title: Free money personality test: what's your money type? — cv.cm
money.description: Free money personality quiz. Rate 20 statements to learn whether you are a saver, spender, investor, avoider or giver, with strengths, blind spots and a tip. No sign-up.
money.lede: Your habits with money say more about your financial future than luck does. Find your money type and the one habit that would help it most.
about: Financial psychologists such as Brad Klontz describe money beliefs we absorb growing up, which quietly drive how we save, spend and invest. This quiz, written for cv.cm, sorts common habits into five money personalities.
No type is good or bad. Each has a strength to use and a blind spot to manage. This quiz cannot predict your fortune: it describes habits, and habits can change.

faq.q: Can this test predict how rich I will be?
faq.a: No. No test can predict fortune. It shows habits that tend to help or hurt your finances over time, which you can change.

faq.q: What are the five money types here?
faq.a: Saver, spender, investor (risk-taker), avoider, and giver.

faq.q: Can I be more than one type?
faq.a: Yes. The chart shows all five. Many people are, for example, a saver with a strong giver side.

faq.q: What should couples do with their results?
faq.a: Compare types. A saver and a spender together can balance each other if they agree on a shared budget.

saver.name: The Saver
saver.body: Strength: discipline, savings and a safety net. Blind spot: you may hold back from spending on things that would really improve your life, or keep cash that could be growing. Tip: set a guilt-free fun budget each month, and put long-term savings into a simple diversified fund.

spender.name: The Spender
spender.body: Strength: you enjoy life and are generous with experiences. Blind spot: impulse buys and little left for the future. Tip: move a fixed amount to savings automatically on payday, and wait 48 hours before any non-essential purchase.

investor.name: The Investor
investor.body: Strength: you spot opportunities and let money work for you. Blind spot: chasing big wins can mean too much risk in one place. Tip: keep an emergency fund first, and never put more into one bet than you can afford to lose.

avoider.name: The Avoider
avoider.body: Strength: money doesn't run your life. Blind spot: unopened bills, late fees and missed chances because looking feels stressful. Tip: book a 15-minute money date each week to check your balance and pay bills; it gets easier fast.

giver.name: The Giver
giver.body: Strength: generosity and strong relationships. Blind spot: giving away what you need for your own security. Tip: decide on a giving budget in advance, so you can be generous without putting your own future at risk.

chronotype.title: Free chronotype test: are you a morning lark or a night owl? — cv.cm
chronotype.description: Free chronotype quiz. Answer 14 questions about your natural sleep and energy rhythm to see if you are a morning lark, a night owl or in between, with practical schedule tips.
chronotype.h1: Chronotype test: morning lark or night owl?
chronotype.lede: Your chronotype is your body clock's natural timing: when you feel sleepy, when you wake, and when you think best. Answer 14 questions about how you live when nobody sets the alarm.
about: Chronotype is partly genetic and changes with age: teenagers and young adults tend to run late, and most people shift earlier after their mid-twenties. Larks feel sharpest in the morning; owls hit their stride in the evening; most people are somewhere in between.

The questions here were written for cv.cm and are not a clinical questionnaire. The result is a self-reflection, not a diagnosis. If you often can't fall asleep, wake up exhausted after a full night, or feel very sleepy during the day, talk to a doctor: those can be signs of a sleep problem that has nothing to do with being an owl.

faq.q: Can a night owl become a morning person?
faq.a: Partly. Your underlying tendency stays, but you can shift your schedule earlier with steady habits: bright light soon after waking, dim light in the evening, and the same wake time every day, moved 15 minutes at a time.

faq.q: Is one chronotype healthier?
faq.a: No chronotype is unhealthy by itself. Problems come from a mismatch: an owl forced into early starts builds up sleep debt. Matching your schedule to your clock where you can, and keeping it regular, matters most.

faq.q: Why do you ask about weekends?
faq.a: Sleeping much later on free days than on workdays, sometimes called social jet lag, is a common sign that your natural clock runs later than your schedule.

faq.q: Is this a sleep disorder test?
faq.a: No. It describes your natural timing. It cannot detect insomnia, sleep apnea or other conditions; see a doctor if sleep problems affect your daily life.

lark.name: Morning lark
lark.body: Your body clock runs early: you wake easily and think best before lunch. Tips: put your hardest work between about 8 a.m. and noon and keep afternoons for meetings and routine tasks; protect your bedtime on nights out, or plan a short afternoon nap instead of a late lie-in; dim screens an hour before bed so you don't wake at 4 a.m. Larks often find late-evening social life tiring: it's fine to suggest brunch instead of drinks.

between.name: In between
between.body: Your clock sits in the middle, like most people's, so you adapt fairly easily to normal schedules. Tips: keep the same wake time every day, weekends included, within about an hour; get daylight in the morning; and notice your own peak, usually late morning, for demanding tasks. A steady routine matters more than which hour you choose.

owl.name: Night owl
owl.body: Your body clock runs late: mornings are hard and you come alive in the evening. Tips: get bright light, outdoors if possible, within an hour of waking, and keep evening light dim and warm; keep wake time within an hour on weekends to limit social jet lag; stop caffeine about eight hours before bed; to shift earlier, move bedtime and wake time by 15 minutes every few days. Ask for later meetings where you can, and put demanding work in the late afternoon.

pet.title: Which pet is right for me? Free pet match quiz — cv.cm
pet.description: Free pet quiz. Answer 14 questions about your time, home, budget, allergies and lifestyle to see whether a cat, dog, rabbit, fish, bird, hamster or reptile suits you best.
pet.lede: A good match makes life better for you and the animal. Answer 14 honest questions about your time, space, money and habits, and see which pet fits your life right now.
about: This quiz, written for cv.cm, weighs the practical things that decide whether an animal will thrive with you: daily time, home size, hours away, travel, allergies, budget, noise, lifespan and the chores you can live with. It is a starting point, not a guarantee: individual animals and breeds vary a lot.

Before you bring any animal home: research the species' needs, count the full cost including vet care, check your lease and local rules, and think about who will care for it when you travel. Consider adopting from a shelter or rescue, and fostering first if you're unsure. A pet is a commitment for its whole life, which can mean decades.

faq.q: What is the easiest pet for a beginner?
faq.a: There is no zero-effort pet. For busy people, a cat or a properly set-up aquarium usually fits best; for families with time and space, a dog. Small animals like hamsters and rabbits need more specialized care than people expect.

faq.q: I'm allergic. Can I still have a pet?
faq.a: Fish and reptiles don't shed fur or dander, so they are the safest choices. No cat or dog is truly hypoallergenic; if you want one, spend time with that animal before adopting and ask a doctor.

faq.q: How much does a pet cost?
faq.a: It depends on the species and where you live. Beyond food, plan for the setup (cage, tank, lamps), vaccinations, neutering, and an emergency vet fund. Reptile and aquarium setups cost more up front than many people expect.

faq.q: Should I get a pet for my child?
faq.a: Only if an adult is ready to be the real caregiver. Children can help, but hamsters and rabbits are fragile and often don't like being held, so supervise every interaction.

cat.name: Cat
cat.body: A cat fits a busy life with moderate space: independent but affectionate, fine alone during a workday, no walks needed. Plan for: 15 or more years, a clean litter box (one per cat plus one), scratching posts, play every day, yearly vet checks, and neutering. Indoor cats live longer; a catio or window perch keeps them entertained.

dog.name: Dog
dog.body: You have the time, space and energy a dog needs, and you want a companion who shares your days. Plan for: 10 to 15 years, walks and play every day, training from day one, someone home or a dog walker on long days, and a bigger budget for food, grooming and vets. Choose energy level and size to match your life, and look at shelters and breed rescues first.

rabbit.name: Rabbit
rabbit.body: A rabbit suits a calm home with floor space and someone around much of the day. Rabbits are social, so most are happiest in a bonded pair, and they need hours of free-roam time in a rabbit-proofed room, not a small hutch. Plan for: 8 to 12 years, unlimited hay, a vet who knows rabbits, and neutering. They rarely enjoy being picked up; enjoy them on their level.

fish.name: Fish
fish.body: An aquarium fits small spaces, tight schedules and allergies, and it's genuinely calming to watch. Skip the bowl: start with a filtered, heated tank of at least 40 liters (about 10 gallons), and cycle it for several weeks before adding fish. Plan for: weekly partial water changes, testing kits, and choosing species that suit the tank size and each other.

bird.name: Bird
bird.body: A bird fits someone home a lot who enjoys interaction and doesn't mind noise. Parrots, even small ones, are smart, social and need hours of time outside the cage, toys to chew and training. Plan for: a long life (budgies 5 to 10 years, larger parrots 30 or more), an avian vet, and a fresh diet beyond seed. If you're away all day, a pair of small birds may be better than one.

hamster.name: Hamster
hamster.body: A hamster fits a small space, a modest budget and a quiet evening routine. They are solitary and nocturnal, so they'll be awake when you're winding down, and their wheel may squeak at night. Plan for: a big enclosure (at least 100 × 50 cm floor), deep bedding to burrow, a solid wheel of the right size, and a 2- to 3-year life. Handle gently; they're not ideal for young children.

reptile.name: Reptile
reptile.body: A reptile fits someone who is curious, patient, allergic to fur, or away often. Many species are quiet and fine alone for a day or two once their setup runs well. Plan for: a proper enclosure with heat and UVB lighting on timers, live or frozen food for many species, an exotic-animal vet, and a long life (leopard geckos 15 to 20 years, tortoises much longer). Choose captive-bred animals and research the species first.

anime.title: Which anime character type are you? Free anime personality quiz — cv.cm
anime.description: Free anime personality quiz: are you a tsundere, kuudere, dandere, deredere, genki, chuunibyou, himedere or reliable senpai? Answer 12 questions to find your archetype. No sign-up.
anime.h1: Which anime character archetype are you?
anime.lede: Tsundere or kuudere? Genki or chuunibyou? Answer 12 everyday questions and find the anime archetype that matches your personality.
about: Anime and manga use well-known character archetypes, often named with Japanese slang ending in -dere (from deredere, lovestruck). Each type mixes a surface attitude with a hidden soft side.
This quiz was written for cv.cm just for fun. It looks at how you react to compliments, friends, leadership and stress, and matches you to the closest of eight popular archetypes.

faq.q: What does tsundere mean?
faq.a: A character who acts cold or prickly (tsun-tsun) but is warm and caring underneath (dere-dere).

faq.q: What is the difference between kuudere and dandere?
faq.a: A kuudere is calm and cool by choice and rarely shows emotion. A dandere is quiet because of shyness and opens up once comfortable.

faq.q: What is chuunibyou?
faq.a: Literally "eighth-grader syndrome": a character who believes in, or acts out, secret powers and dramatic destinies.

faq.q: Is this quiz serious?
faq.a: No. It is a fun personality quiz. For a research-based profile, take the Big Five test.

tsundere.name: Tsundere
tsundere.body: Prickly on the outside, soft on the inside. You hide affection behind teasing and denial, but your loyalty is fierce and your kindness shows in actions. The people who know you best find it adorable.

kuudere.name: Kuudere
kuudere.body: Cool, calm and composed. You rarely show emotion and think before you act, which makes you the steady one in a crisis. When you do smile, people remember it.

dandere.name: Dandere
dandere.body: Quiet and shy around new people, warm and funny once you feel safe. You notice everything and care deeply, even if it takes a while for others to see it.

deredere.name: Deredere
deredere.body: Sweet, cheerful and openly affectionate. You love freely, cheer people on and brighten every room. Your kindness is your superpower.

genki.name: Genki
genki.body: Energetic, upbeat and always ready for the next adventure. You pull friends out of their comfort zones and make ordinary days exciting.

chuuni.name: Chuunibyou
chuuni.body: Dramatic, imaginative and full of grand narratives. Your inner world is epic, and you turn everyday life into a story worth telling. Never lose that creativity.

himedere.name: Himedere
himedere.body: Confident, elegant and used to being treated like royalty. You set high standards and carry yourself with style, and underneath you're loyal to the people who earn your trust.

senpai.name: Reliable senpai
senpai.body: Dependable, mature and protective. You give good advice, keep the group together and look out for everyone, like the senpai every protagonist needs.

face-shape.title: Face shape test: what is my face shape? Free quiz — cv.cm
face-shape.description: Free face shape test. Answer 6 questions with a mirror to find whether your face is oval, round, square, heart, oblong, diamond or triangle, with hairstyle and glasses tips. No photo upload.
face-shape.lede: Find your face shape with a mirror and 6 quick questions, then get hairstyle, glasses and grooming tips that suit it. No photo needed, nothing uploaded.
about: How to look: pull your hair back, stand in front of a mirror (or take a straight-on selfie), and compare four things: face length, forehead width, cheekbone width and jaw width. A soft tape measure or a piece of string makes it easier.
Most faces are a mix of two shapes, so the quiz also shows how close you are to each. Face shape is about proportions, not beauty: every shape has styles that flatter it.

faq.q: How do I measure my face shape?
faq.a: Measure forehead width at the hairline, cheekbone width at the widest point, jaw width from the corner under each ear to the chin, and length from hairline to chin. Then answer the questions.

faq.q: What is the most common face shape?
faq.a: Oval and round are often cited as the most common, but many people are a blend of two shapes.

faq.q: Does the test use my photo?
faq.a: No. You answer from a mirror or your own photo; nothing is uploaded or analyzed.

faq.q: Can makeup or a beard change my face shape?
faq.a: They change how it looks. Contouring, hairstyles and beard shape add or soften angles to balance proportions.

oval.name: Oval face
oval.body: Balanced proportions: a little longer than wide, with a jaw slightly narrower than the forehead. Almost any hairstyle and frame shape works. Try bold or geometric glasses, and both short and long cuts.

round.name: Round face
round.body: Similar length and width, with full cheeks and a soft jaw. Add height and angles: layered cuts with volume on top, side parts, and rectangular or angular glasses. Avoid blunt chin-length bobs and round frames.

square.name: Square face
square.body: Strong, angular jaw with forehead, cheeks and jaw of similar width. Soften the corners: soft layers, side-swept bangs and waves; round or oval glasses. Short beards that round the chin work well.

heart.name: Heart face
heart.body: Wider forehead and cheekbones narrowing to a pointed chin. Balance the lower face: chin-length bobs, side bangs and volume near the jaw; bottom-heavy or rimless glasses. A fuller beard adds width at the chin.

oblong.name: Oblong face
oblong.body: Clearly longer than wide, with forehead, cheeks and jaw of similar width. Add width: bangs, waves and volume at the sides; oversized or deep frames. Avoid very long straight hair and tall styling on top.

diamond.name: Diamond face
diamond.body: Wide, high cheekbones with a narrower forehead and jaw. Show off the cheekbones: side-swept fringes, tucked-behind-the-ear styles and chin-length cuts; oval or cat-eye glasses.

triangle.name: Triangle (pear) face
triangle.body: Jaw wider than the forehead. Add width up top: volume at the crown and temples, layered cuts, side bangs; frames that are bold on top, like browline glasses. Keep beards short at the sides.

self-esteem.title: Free self-esteem test (Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale) — cv.cm
self-esteem.description: Take the Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale online for free. 10 statements, an instant score out of 30 and what it means. No sign-up, answers stay in your browser.
self-esteem.lede: The Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale is the most widely used measure of self-worth. Rate 10 statements and get a score out of 30.
about: Sociologist Morris Rosenberg published the scale in 1965, and it has been used in thousands of studies since. Five statements are positive and five are negative; the negative ones are reverse-scored.
Scores from 15 to 25 are in the typical range. A score below 15 suggests low self-esteem. Self-esteem changes with life events, and it can be built with practice and support.

faq.q: How is the Rosenberg scale scored?
faq.a: Each answer scores 0 to 3, with items 2, 5, 6, 8 and 9 reversed. The total runs from 0 to 30; higher means higher self-esteem.

faq.q: What is a normal score?
faq.a: Most people score between 15 and 25. Below 15 suggests low self-esteem.

faq.q: How can I improve my self-esteem?
faq.a: Notice and challenge harsh self-talk, keep small promises to yourself, spend time with supportive people, and talk to a counselor if low self-worth affects daily life.

faq.q: Is a high score always good?
faq.a: Healthy self-esteem is realistic. A very high score is usually fine, but self-worth that depends on always being better than others is fragile.

low.name: Lower self-esteem
low.body: Your score suggests you are often hard on yourself. That is painful, and it is common. Try writing down three things you did well each day, notice when your inner voice is harsher than you would be to a friend, and consider talking with a counselor.

normal.name: Typical self-esteem
normal.body: Your score is in the typical range: you generally accept yourself while recognizing room to grow. Keep up habits that support you, like time with people who value you and goals you can reach.

high.name: High self-esteem
high.body: You have a strong, positive view of yourself. Healthy self-esteem helps you handle setbacks and set boundaries. Keep it grounded by staying open to feedback.

anxiety.title: Free anxiety test (GAD-7): check your anxiety level — cv.cm
anxiety.description: Free GAD-7 anxiety test online. Answer 7 questions about the last two weeks and get your score from 0 to 21 with the standard severity level. Private: nothing leaves your browser.
anxiety.lede: The GAD-7 is a 7-question screening tool doctors use to check for generalized anxiety. It takes about a minute and scores from 0 to 21.
about: The Generalized Anxiety Disorder 7-item scale (GAD-7) was developed by Spitzer, Kroenke, Williams and Löwe in 2006. It is free to use and is widely used in primary care. Scores of 5, 10 and 15 mark mild, moderate and severe anxiety.
A score of 10 or more is a reason to talk to a doctor or mental health professional. This check is a screening tool, not a diagnosis.

faq.q: What does my GAD-7 score mean?
faq.a: 0–4 minimal, 5–9 mild, 10–14 moderate and 15–21 severe anxiety symptoms over the last two weeks.

faq.q: Can the GAD-7 diagnose anxiety disorder?
faq.a: No. It screens for symptoms. A diagnosis needs an assessment by a qualified professional.

faq.q: When should I seek help?
faq.a: If your score is 10 or more, or if anxiety gets in the way of work, school, sleep or relationships, talk to a doctor or counselor.

faq.q: What helps with anxiety?
faq.a: Regular sleep, exercise, less caffeine, slow breathing and talking to someone you trust help many people. Therapy (such as CBT) and medication are effective treatments.

items: Feeling nervous, anxious, or on edge
Not being able to stop or control worrying
Worrying too much about different things
Trouble relaxing
Being so restless that it is hard to sit still
Becoming easily annoyed or irritable
Feeling afraid as if something awful might happen

minimal.name: Minimal anxiety (0–4)
minimal.body: Your answers suggest few or no anxiety symptoms over the last two weeks. Keep up the habits that help you stay balanced.

mild.name: Mild anxiety (5–9)
mild.body: You have some anxiety symptoms. Watch how they develop, and try stress-reducing habits like regular sleep, exercise and limiting caffeine. Retake the test in a few weeks.

moderate.name: Moderate anxiety (10–14)
moderate.body: Your symptoms are at a level where talking to a doctor or mental health professional is recommended. Anxiety is very treatable.

severe.name: Severe anxiety (15–21)
severe.body: Your answers suggest severe anxiety symptoms. Please reach out to a doctor or mental health professional soon. You don't have to handle this alone, and effective help exists.

depression.title: Free depression test (PHQ-9): depression screening — cv.cm
depression.description: Free PHQ-9 depression test online. Answer 9 questions about the last two weeks for a score from 0 to 27 and the standard severity level. Private: nothing leaves your browser.
depression.lede: The PHQ-9 is the 9-question depression screening used by doctors worldwide. It takes about two minutes and scores from 0 to 27.
about: The Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-9) was developed by Kroenke, Spitzer and Williams and is free to use. Scores of 5, 10, 15 and 20 mark mild, moderate, moderately severe and severe depression symptoms.
A score of 10 or more is a reason to see a doctor or mental health professional. If you have any thoughts of hurting yourself, reach out for help now, whatever your total score.

faq.q: What does my PHQ-9 score mean?
faq.a: 0–4 minimal, 5–9 mild, 10–14 moderate, 15–19 moderately severe and 20–27 severe depression symptoms.

faq.q: Can the PHQ-9 diagnose depression?
faq.a: No. It is a screening tool. A doctor or mental health professional makes a diagnosis after a full assessment.

faq.q: Why does question 9 matter so much?
faq.a: It asks about thoughts of death or self-harm. Any answer other than "not at all" deserves a conversation with a professional, even if the total score is low.

faq.q: Is depression treatable?
faq.a: Yes. Therapy, medication, exercise and social support all help, and most people improve with treatment.

items: Little interest or pleasure in doing things
Feeling down, depressed, or hopeless
Trouble falling or staying asleep, or sleeping too much
Feeling tired or having little energy
Poor appetite or overeating
Feeling bad about yourself, or that you are a failure or have let yourself or your family down
Trouble concentrating on things, such as reading or watching television
Moving or speaking so slowly that other people could have noticed, or the opposite: being so fidgety or restless that you have been moving around a lot more than usual
Thoughts that you would be better off dead, or of hurting yourself in some way

minimal.name: Minimal depression (0–4)
minimal.body: Your answers suggest few or no symptoms of depression over the last two weeks.

mild.name: Mild depression (5–9)
mild.body: You have some symptoms. Keep an eye on how you feel, look after sleep, movement and social contact, and retake the test in a few weeks. If it doesn't improve, talk to a doctor.

moderate.name: Moderate depression (10–14)
moderate.body: Your symptoms are at a level where seeing a doctor or mental health professional is recommended. Depression is common and treatable.

modsevere.name: Moderately severe depression (15–19)
modsevere.body: Your answers suggest significant symptoms. Please contact a doctor or mental health professional soon. Treatment such as therapy and medication helps most people.

severe.name: Severe depression (20–27)
severe.body: Your answers suggest severe symptoms. Please reach out to a doctor or mental health professional as soon as possible, and let someone you trust know how you are feeling.
